content.text:
I submitted **holistic** with confidence 0.9. I used 38 of the 60 budget.

**How I set it up:** I trained the learner on two tasks, L1-S1-M1 and L2-S2-M2. Then I tested tasks where the two hypotheses predict different orderings: some reuse only rules the learner already knows, some add a new rule, and their mappings are either close to or far from the trained tasks.

| Test task | New rules | Highest similarity to a trained task | Mean examples (number of tests) |
|---|---|---|---|
| L2-S2-M1 | 0 | 0.75 | ~5 (7) |
| L1-S1-M3 | 1 | 0.75 | ~19 (11) |
| L1-S1-M2 | 0 | 0.375 | ~28 (14) |
| L4-S4-M4 | 3 | ~0.06 | ~40 (4) |

**What the results show:**
- **The two tasks with no new rules differed by a factor of about 5.** L2-S2-M1 and L1-S1-M2 both use only known rules, so the part-based hypothesis says they should cost the same. They didn't: the one whose mapping is closer to the trained tasks was much faster.
- **A task with a new rule was faster than one without.** L1-S1-M3 has one new rule but a similar mapping, and it beat L1-S1-M2, which has no new rules but a dissimilar mapping. Part-based predicts the reverse.
- **Mapping similarity explains the costs, whatever the number of new rules.** L1-S1-M2 (no new rules) cost about as much as L4-S4-M4, which has three.

Single tests were very noisy (one task ranged from 1 to 37 examples), so I repeated each test several times. The main differences were still clear.
